reason: The Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only, but its progress statements of 2024, 2025 and 2026 turn on the bilateral social security agreements, moving from limited progress in 2023 and 2024 to good progress in 2025 and 2026. The issue's own items show agreements added in each year: Spain signed and Greece in force by 2023, Spain and Latvia in force in 2024, Italy and France signed in October 2024 and March 2025, Italy in force in September 2025 and Slovakia signed in March 2026.

The Commission asked in each report from 2023 to 2026 for further social security coordination agreements with Member States, adding in 2026 a request for gap analyses on the coordination regulations, and it reports in 2026 that negotiations with other Member States should continue. The Government reported in 2025 agreements with 17 of the 27 Member States, its own count, and the Slovakia agreement signed in March 2026 is not yet reported in force. What remains is agreements with the Member States not yet covered, entry into force of those signed, and the gap analyses on the coordination regulations.

Concluding further agreements with Member States is a key recommendation in all four Commission reports from 2023 to 2026, and the Chapter 2 progress statements of 2024 to 2026 rest on it, so it is central to the chapter. Agreements have been added each year, but the recommendation is still repeated in 2026.

The Commission records agreements signed or brought into force in every year from 2023 to 2026, negotiated by an established institution, the National Social Insurance House. The Government itself says it cannot commit to a number of agreements because the pace depends on the political will of the other states, so completion is not in Moldova's hands alone.

The Chapter 2 rating covers more than this issue and is context only. The 2023 report and Analytical Report found the preparatory work for EURES not completed, the 2024 report recorded its start with an action plan and the National Employment Agency designated as coordination body, and the 2025 report recorded a EURES department and the September 2025 Government Decision setting the national legal framework. The 2026 report adds the National Coordination Office, the procedure for admitting members and partners, 10 territorial EURES members, implementing acts on data and monitoring and technical standards for matching with the EURES portal.

The Commission asked in 2023, 2024 and 2025 for the preparatory work for EURES to continue, and in 2026 it records the legal framework, coordination office and admission procedure as in place. The Government describes its 2024 and 2025 Decisions as only partial transposition of the EURES Regulation, says data exchange with the European platform and legislative alignment still need to be completed, and lists further agency orders, including on interoperability with EURES, as planned. What remains is completing legal alignment with the EURES Regulation and the technical connection and data exchange with the EURES platform, ahead of membership on accession.

Preparing to join EURES was a key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, which on its own would point to High. No item among the 41 Moldova items on this issue repeats the recommendation in 2026, when the Commission records the main legal and organisational steps as taken, and membership itself comes only with accession, so the issue is weighed as Medium.

The work lies mainly with one body, the National Employment Agency, and uses Government Decisions and agency orders; the steps planned in 2024 and 2025 were reported as taken by the Commission in the following report. The remaining technical connection depends on the employment service's IT capacity, which the 2025 recommendation asks Moldova to reinforce.

No item among the six Moldova items on this issue is EU standard-scale wording or an EU requirement; the only EU item, from 2026, reports that a feasibility study on introducing the European Health Insurance Card was carried out. The Government stated in 2025 that the EU acts on the Card are not transposed, and two points in time with no assessed change are not enough to set a direction.

The Government stated in 2025 that the EU acts on the European Health Insurance Card are not transposed and listed applying the Card and a draft law on cross-border medical care as planned. The Commission reported in 2026 only that a feasibility study had been carried out. What remains is a decision on introducing the Card and the legal and financial arrangements that would give EU citizens access to healthcare through it.

The Card is part of the Chapter 2 acquis on social security coordination, but the Commission names it in the 2025 key recommendation only as IT infrastructure to be developed, alongside the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. It is not a repeated key recommendation in the items held for this issue and for RI-FMW-008, which keeps it below High.

Preparation has started: a feasibility study on the Card's impact on public finances was completed and a draft law on cross-border medical care is planned. The study's focus on public finances points to cost as the main constraint, and the international cooperation section dealing with Member State institutions has three specialists.

The issue rests on a single Moldova item, a 2026 civil society report that illegal surveys in the parliamentary election campaign used personal data databases of unclear origin. It is not raised in EU material, and one item from one year cannot show a direction.

The single item held is a civil society finding, with no EU requirement and no intervention responding to it, so the gap cannot be measured against what the EU requires. What remains is, on that one report, oversight of how personal data are obtained, stored and used in election campaigns, which other sources would need to confirm.
The issue is raised only by one civil society source and not in EU material, which keeps priority from being High. With a single item and no EU recommendation or benchmark, it is Low.
The single item names no responsible institution and no past action on the issue, so how realistic progress would be cannot be judged.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, as this issue comes from a cross-cutting theme and was not decisive. SIGMA found in 2023 that government websites complied poorly with WCAG 2.0 despite guidelines, with an average of 45 errors per page across 26 tested sites, and the Commission found in 2026 that public sector websites and mobile applications remain insufficiently accessible and that accessibility is insufficiently enforced and funded.

The 2026 key recommendation asks Moldova to improve the accessibility of public sector websites and mobile applications. The law on accessibility requirements for products and services adopted in August 2026, which the Commission describes as in line with the acquis, is a legal step for products and services, while the order setting WCAG 2.2 rules for public websites had not started in 2026 because it awaits a Government Decision. What remains is binding accessibility rules for public sector websites and applications and their enforcement and funding.

Accessibility of public sector websites and applications is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, the first Commission report among the 14 Moldova items on this issue to raise it, and no item on the issue names it in a Reform Agenda payment condition. It is a clear EU requirement but not yet repeated across reports.

Guidelines for government websites already exist, and the WCAG 2.2 rules are a single order of the e-Governance Agency once the Government Decision is approved. The poor compliance SIGMA found across many sites in 2023 and the Commission's finding that accessibility is insufficiently enforced and funded show that bringing existing sites into line needs resources across many institutions.

Sub-area wording on the 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, which matches this issue, recorded no progress in 2024. The Commission asked in 2025 for implementation of the Toolbox measures to continue and in 2026 for Moldova to start implementing them, including restrictions on high-risk suppliers, so the core requirement is unchanged across the three reports; the secondary legislation on security of public 5G networks noted in 2026 and the supplier risk study under way are preparatory steps.

The 2026 report asks Moldova to start implementing the Toolbox measures, including restrictions or exclusions for high-risk suppliers, which the Reform Agenda also sets as a step. The Government reports a supplier risk assessment by a consultancy still in progress and a draft 5G security law still being finalised in 2026, with the law planned by December 2027. What remains is the 5G security law, the completed supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers applied to critical assets.

Alignment with the 5G Toolbox is part of the key recommendation on the Digital Transformation Strategy priorities in the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports and is a step of the Reform Agenda under the Reform and Growth Facility, after the sub-area recorded no progress in 2024. It is central to the cybersecurity theme.

Funded preparatory work is under way, with a study funded by Swedfund and a consultancy contract covering supplier risk assessment, an operator compensation mechanism and a draft law. The Government notes that compliance requires major investment in 5G networks, so progress depends on operators bearing, or being compensated for, the cost of restricting high-risk suppliers.

The Chapter 29 rating covers more than this issue and is context only; it recorded good progress in 2025 and 2026, naming the New Computerised Transit System both times. The issue's own items move from uncertainty about the transit system in 2021 and requests for an IT strategy in 2023 and 2024, to migration to NCTS Phase 5 in October 2024, Phase 6 in September 2025, full accession to the Common Transit Convention in November 2025 and a fully operational Customs Decisions System by June 2026.

The 2026 report asks Moldova to adopt the Customs Code amendments that give the legal basis for EU-interoperable IT systems and to advance the national customs IT programme approved in October 2025, of whose 25 systems three are operational. The Commission notes that implementation remains incomplete because of transitional provisions and a lack of IT tools, and the Government states that the programme has no budget coverage. What remains is the Customs Code amendments and most of the programme's systems, including the core interconnectivity systems and a Single Window Environment for Customs.

Customs IT is a key recommendation in every Commission report from 2023 to 2026, and accession to the Common Transit Convention, the transit system and the Customs Decisions System are steps of the Reform Agenda. Interoperability with the EU electronic customs environment is central to the customs chapter and to the interoperability theme.

The Customs Service delivered the transit system, Convention accession and the Customs Decisions System close to the dates set, the Commission judged the related Reform Agenda steps satisfactorily fulfilled, and EU expert support continues. The lack of budget coverage for the 2025 to 2030 programme, reported by the Government, is the main risk to keeping that pace.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, as this issue is part of the AI theme and the scale was not decisive. The Government recorded a lack of legal acts on AI in 2023, the Commission found in 2025 that Moldova is not yet aligned with the AI Act and in 2026 asked it to develop governance, regulatory and enforcement structures, and the Government's 2026 programme document still describes the field as at an early stage with no competent authority or AI-specific framework. The 2024 White Paper is declarative, and a 2026 civil society report says the AI sub-council produced no legislative initiative.

The Commission requires governance, regulatory and enforcement structures in line with the AI Act. A draft AI law, a law on AI testing spaces, the 2026 to 2030 national programme and an AI governance institution are all planned or being drafted, and the Government reported in 2025 that no institution responsible for AI policy or supervision had been identified. What remains is a law aligned with the AI Act, a designated and staffed supervisory authority, and the governance structure to apply it.

AI Act alignment is raised by the Commission in 2025 as a finding and in 2026 as a recommendation, and no item among the 108 Moldova items on this issue names it in a benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. It is central to the AI theme but not yet repeated across three reports.

The National Accession Programme plans transposition of the AI Act and a governance institution by 2027, and a consultative sub-council exists. In 2025 no ministry employee covered AI policy, the competent authority was yet to be chosen, and funding for the national programme depends on the annual budget process.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. The Commission found the 2022 law partially aligned with eIDAS in 2023, found full alignment with eIDAS 1.0 in 2025 with the European Digital Identity framework to follow, and in 2026 found an advanced level of alignment after the December 2025 amendments on qualified trust service providers. The improvement is legal, and sources conflict on when Law No. 124/2022 entered into force: 10 December 2022 in the 2023 report, 1 January 2025 according to the Government.

The Commission asked in 2024 for interoperability with the European Digital Identity Wallets, and the Reform Agenda expects alignment with eIDAS 2 and an EU-aligned national wallet by December 2026. In 2026 the law transposing eIDAS 2 was still being drafted, a set of implementing orders on the wallet framework was planned, and the national wallet was under development since September 2025. What remains is the eIDAS 2 law and its implementing acts, and a national digital identity wallet interoperable with the European Digital Identity Wallets.

Alignment with EU electronic identification requirements was part of the 2024 key recommendation, and alignment with eIDAS 2 with an EU-aligned national wallet is a step of the Reform Agenda due by December 2026. It is central to the electronic identification theme.

Moldova moved from partial to advanced alignment between 2023 and 2026, with amending laws in 2025 and technical assistance under EU4Digital for eIDAS 2. Staffing is thin, with one ministry post on trust services and the capacity of the ministry and regulator named as needs, which may slow the remaining implementing acts.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. The 2023 report recorded adoption of the Law on cybersecurity but said implementation had to start, the 2024 and 2025 reports recorded implementing Government Decisions aimed at NIS 2 alignment, and the 2026 report records further secondary legislation and the National Cybersecurity Programme 2026-2030 adopted in December 2025, replacing the strategy the Reform Agenda had described as lapsed. The improvement is mainly legal and strategic, as the Reform Agenda still found no holistic framework in 2025.

The key recommendation of 2024, 2025 and 2026 asks Moldova to align legislation with EU cybersecurity standards. The Government describes Law No. 48/2023 as only partially harmonising with NIS 2, and the amending law for NIS 2, the laws on the Cyber Resilience Act and cybersecurity certification and the related authority designations were still planned in 2025 and 2026. What remains is full transposition of NIS 2 and of the Cyber Resilience Act and certification framework, with the authorities designated to apply them.

Alignment with EU cybersecurity standards is in the key recommendation of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and NIS 2 alignment with clarified institutional roles is part of the Reform Agenda. The legal framework is central to the cybersecurity theme.

Moldova has adopted the main law and a series of implementing Government Decisions since 2023, which shows legislative capacity. The Cybersecurity Agency reports that missing staff and an incomplete framework limited supervision in 2025, the ministry's cybersecurity unit has four posts with one vacant, and the Reform Agenda expects compliance costs to meet resistance from operators.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only. In 2021 the national CERT was pending approval of its mandate, in 2024 and 2025 the Commission asked for further effort on the operational capacity of the new Cybersecurity Agency, and the Reform Agenda found it short of staff, IT resources and legal authority. In 2026 the Commission reports the Agency operational as single point of contact and national CERT, with 32 staff by December 2025 and an incident platform in use, and judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled.

The Reform Agenda step on making the Agency fully operational with a national CERT is judged fulfilled, but the Agency's 2025 report says supervision was only partly carried out for lack of staff and a complete framework, its SIEM and incident playbooks were incomplete, and it lacks qualified IT specialists. The Government reports that cyber incidents rose by over 30 percent between 2021 and 2023, and the 2026 report notes security vulnerabilities in the border police information system. What remains is enough qualified staff and tools for the Agency and CERT to supervise providers and protect state systems.

Operational capacity of the Agency was named in the 2024 and 2025 reports and in a Reform Agenda step, which would point to High, but the Commission judged that step satisfactorily fulfilled and no item among the 216 Moldova items on this issue repeats the requirement in a 2026 Commission recommendation. The issue stays central to the cybersecurity theme, so it is weighed as Medium.

The Agency went from its launch in 2024 to an operational CERT in 2025, with substantial EU and bilateral support in experts, equipment, software and training. The Agency names recruitment of qualified specialists and limited own resources for equipment as its constraints.
